newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's M1 up a sharp 3.4 percent in January.
newsitem.headline: Israel's M1 up a sharp 3.4 percent in January.

text.p: Israel's M1 money supply grew a sharp 3.4 percent in January to 17.56 billion shekels, following a 1.8 percent rise in December, according to preliminary figures from the Bank of Israel released on Sunday.
Total credit rose 1.6 percent in January to 255 billion shekels, led by a 2.9 percent increase in unlinked-shekel lending to 83.4 billion shekels.
Money supply is one of the factors the Bank of Israel uses to determine interest rates. It is due to announce its March monetary programme on February 24.

The January M1 increase is the sharpest since last July, when it rose 4.1 percent. For all of 1996, M1 rose 11.8 percent, which Bank of Israel officials have said was appropriate in relation to inflation and economic growth.
The current rates puts the January year-on-year rise at 14.6 percent.

The M1 figure follows the release of an encouraging January consumer price index on Friday, which rose 0.4 percent. The increase was slightly under what government and private sector economists had predicted.
Nevertheless, they said it was unlikely the central bank would cut the base rate, which was lowered to 14.2 percent at the end of January.

The Bank of Israel has been injecting liquidity into the economy in its bid to prevent the currency basket exchange rate from moving below its official trading band. In addition, the government ran an unexpectedly big deficit of 1.28 billion shekels in January.
But Bank of Israel governor Jacob Frenkel insisted last week the central bank was absorbing the excess liquidity.

Jonathan Katz, chief economist on Solid Financial Markets, said he suspected the M1 rise was due to a movement of money into current accounts because interest rates have been coming down since mid-1996 and because of the stock market rally.
"The public is willing to keep more money liquid," Katz said.
